title: Your rule of life
hookLine: write down your own daily practice
tomorrow: the five prayers are fixed. so how does a busy day fit them?

cards: A planner app full of color-coded blocks, abandoned by Wednesday. Fresh starts often look like that: too much, too fast, gone. Two very different houses of prayer wrote down an answer to it.
Christian monks who live by the Rule of Saint Benedict order their days on paper: hours for prayer, for work, for reading. And Muslims have a word for a personal daily set of devotion: a wird.
Same question underneath: how do you build a practice that lasts?

teach.b: The Islamic answer is small and steady. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says the deeds most beloved to God are the ones done regularly, even if they're small.
And 'A'isha, asked how the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ kept his devotions, described them as constant, the way steady rain keeps falling. Now the neighbor, in its own words.

The Rule of Saint Benedict opens by hoping to set down nothing harsh and nothing burdensome. Later it says idleness is the enemy of the soul, so the day gets its hours: prayer, work with the hands, holy reading.
Different language, a shared instinct: keep it gentle, keep it regular, and write it down so a bad day doesn't erase it. And one honest difference.
Benedict wrote for monks living together under an abbot, their day kept by the community's bell.

teach.h: A MONASTERY, OR AN ORDINARY HOUSE.
teach.b: A Muslim's rule is lived in an ordinary house, school or job, and its spine is already set: the five daily prayers.
The personal part, the wird, is built around them: a few verses after dawn, a remembrance at night. Neither needs the other to be wrong.
One to tell a friend tonight: a monk's rule and a hadith both say small and steady beats big and brief.

how: Some Muslims keep a wird, a personal daily set of Qur'an, remembrance or prayer, sometimes taken on with a teacher's advice and fitted around the five daily prayers.

games.q: what does “your rule of life” mean?
o: your daily practice, written down and small enough to keep
a vow taken once in life that can never be changed
a strict set of laws a whole community must obey

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.

s: a practice that lasts needs a big start
the hadith: deeds most beloved to God are regular, even if small.
the Rule of Saint Benedict hopes to set down nothing harsh or burdensome
its prologue says so; a monk's rule and a hadith share that instinct.
a wird replaces the five daily prayers
the five prayers are the spine; the wird is built around them.

games.q: your friend wants to start running and signs up for a marathon next month. she's never run a mile. she asks for advice. what fits today?
o: go all in. a big goal is what gets a practice going.
start with a short run most days, and build from there.
wait until she feels motivated, so the practice is sincere.
games.why: small and steady: the hadith prefers regular deeds even if small, and Benedict's Rule hoped for nothing harsh. a habit lasts when it fits the worst day.

practice: On a piece of paper, write three short lines: one thing for the morning, one for the day, one for the night. Make each small enough to keep on your worst day. Read them back once, slowly, and leave them where you'll see them.

wordCard.voice: Your rule of life: your daily practice, written down, small and steady. A personal daily portion of devotion is called a wird.

orig.note: Arabic: a personal daily portion of Qur'an, remembrance or prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: my practice. Small enough to keep, written where you'll see it. One of ten for your own practice.
